entries.title: Benchmarking VLM Medical Hallucination across 5 Modalities
entries.abstract: Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) within the medical domain remain a difficult and not well-understood problem, and it is still unclear where these models break down. Although several benchmarks targeting medical hallucination have been introduced, they often lack broad coverage across different medical imaging modalities. We introduce Multi-Med, a medical hallucination benchmark containing 1,000 image-question pairs spanning five distinct modalities. Using this benchmark, we perform an in-depth experimental study of 10 widely used VLMs across five modalities and four question categories. Our findings indicate that model performance differs substantially depending on the imaging modality and question type, and that the differences among the best-performing models are not statistically significant.

entries.title: Diagnostic specificity of a retrieval augmented language model on complex clinical cases: a retrospective benchmark study
entries.abstract: Background Diagnostic benchmarks can reward recognition of a disease family without requiring the specificity of the final diagnosis. We evaluated the separation between broad diagnostic concordance and strict diagnostic correctness in a retrieval augmented language model. Methods This retrospective benchmark evaluated MediDx AI, which couples Claude Sonnet 4.6 with retrieval from seven biomedical sources without fine-tuning, on presentation-only text from 100 consecutive published Massachusetts General Hospital Case Records, issued from 26 October 2023 to 11 June 2026. Published expert discussions, final diagnoses, source tables and images were withheld. Five ranked suggestions were adjudicated under broad concordance and strict correct, partial or incorrect scoring. Case-level proportions and Wilson 95% confidence intervals were calculated. A separate evaluation used 1,273 medical multiple-choice questions, counting unanswered questions as incorrect. Results Broad top-ranked concordance was 71% (95% confidence interval 61.5–79.0%), whereas 53% (43.3–62.5%) of top-ranked diagnoses were strictly correct; 19% were partial and 28% incorrect. Within five suggestions, broad concordance was 88% and strict correctness was 63%. The 18 broadly concordant but partial top-ranked diagnoses accounted for the difference between the two top-ranked outcomes. Failures included missed causative organisms, rare neoplasms and structural conditions; partial responses often omitted an underlying mechanism or a component of a multicomponent diagnosis. Medical question-answering accuracy was 86.5% across all submitted questions, compared with 92.0% among parseable responses; response coverage was 94.0%. Conclusions Broad diagnostic concordance and strict diagnostic correctness describe different aspects of performance. Reporting both, alongside ranked inclusion and response completion, exposes information concealed by aggregate accuracy. These results do not establish the incremental benefit of retrieval or clinical effectiveness, which require controlled evaluation.

entries.title: From benchmarking to application: a scalable mitochondrial DNA analysis and variant identification framework for whole-genome sequencing
entries.abstract:
Purpose: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variants are implicated in a wide range of diseases. The increasing availability of whole-genome sequencing enables mtDNA analysis in large-scale clinical and population studies. However, optimal tools for accurate variant detection from short-read data remain unclear.

Methods:

We systematically benchmarked four scalable mtDNA variant calling tools: MitoHPC, mtSwirl, mity, and mtDNA-Server 2. Using 1000 Genomes Project (1KG) data and simulations across diverse haplogroups, we evaluated performance in detecting homoplasmic and heteroplasmic variants. Using the optimal tool, we built MARVel (https://github.com/bahlolab/MARVel), an integrated workflow combining variant calling, automated quality-control reporting, and interactive variant curation, including an mtDNA principal component reference from 1KG that captures haplogroup structure and enables projection of external cohorts. We then applied MARVel to an independent ataxia cohort to assess research utility.

Results:

MitoHPC and mtSwirl showed the strongest overall performance, particularly in non-European populations, with MitoHPC preferred for its ease of implementation. mity excelled in detecting low variant allele frequency single nucleotide variants (SNVs) but underperformed for insertions/deletions and showed inconsistent multi-nucleotide polymorphism normalisation. mtDNA-Server 2 maximised SNV sensitivity but had a higher false-positive rate and missed variants in the MT-RNR2 region. Applying MARVel (MitoHPC) to the ataxia cohort recovered known pathogenic mtDNA variants and identified additional candidates for investigation.

Conclusion:

We provide guidance for mtDNA tool selection in large-scale sequencing studies, along with a reproducible benchmarking framework for future evaluation as methods evolve. We also developed MARVel to facilitate disease-associated mtDNA variant discovery and reporting, supporting robust and scalable mtDNA analysis.
